title: Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42)
hook: Martha is busy and cross; Mary sits at his feet; one thing is needed

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lawyer asked who is my neighbor, and a Samaritan answered with oil, wine and his own animal. Your line was go and do likewise. Who turned out to be your neighbor? Day five hundred forty-two.

Luke tells this story in five verses, and he puts it straight after the good Samaritan. That placement matters. Yesterday's hero was the man who stopped and did something. Today, a guest arrives at a house in a village, and the person doing everything gets a gentle word. Luke says a woman named Martha received him into her house. Her house, her welcome, her guest. Luke only says there was much serving; it isn't hard to imagine bread to bake and water to carry. And her sister Mary is sitting on the floor, listening. Anyone who has been the one at the sink while others laugh in the next room may recognize Martha.
screen: `ONE AT THE SINK, ONE ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, Mary "sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word." That phrase is bigger than it sounds. Sitting at a teacher's feet was the place of a student; Paul later says he was brought up at the feet of Gamaliel. Mary takes that place, one some readers think was usually kept for men, and nobody sends her back to the kitchen. Martha, meanwhile, "was cumbered about much serving." Luke's Greek word has the sense of being pulled around, drawn in every direction. Finally she comes in and says: "Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me." Notice she doesn't speak to Mary. She goes over her head. And the answer is gentle. He says her name twice, the way you do with someone you love: "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her." Careful here means full of care, anxious. He doesn't tell Martha to stop cooking. He doesn't call serving wrong; one story earlier, the Samaritan was all service. What he names is the worry, the many things crowding out the one. Christians have read the sisters in more than one way. Some early writers saw two callings, the active life and the quiet life of prayer, and monasteries tried to keep both. Others say every person has a Martha and a Mary inside. And Martha gets her own great moment later: in John's Gospel, she is the one who tells Jesus plainly that she believes he is the Christ. Nobody here is the villain. One sister just needed to sit down first.

Here's the practice: sit before you serve. Before the next thing on your list, stop and sit down, the way Mary did, as if someone worth listening to were in the room. Let the list wait. Notice the many things pulling at you. Name two or three of them, and set each one down for these two minutes. If you pray, you can simply listen, without asking for anything. If you don't, listen to the quiet, to your breath, to whatever is actually here. When the bell rings, get up and serve, but from having sat first. The bell holds the time.
Martha. The sister who welcomed Jesus into her home and was pulled in every direction by much serving, while Mary sat at his feet and listened.
Your line: one thing is needful. Today, when you feel dragged in every direction, stop for a breath and ask what the one thing is, right now. Day five hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Some Christians keep a short time of quiet prayer or Bible reading before the day's work begins, and in monastic communities, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican, the day is shaped by set hours of prayer between hours of work.

original.note: Greek: she was pulled around, distracted. Luke's word for Martha with much serving; the King James Bible says cumbered.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary is the good sister and Martha is the bad one.
what it means: Jesus names Martha's worry, not her work, and invites her to the one thing first.
what a scholar hears: Mary takes a student's place at a teacher's feet, and early Christian writers read the sisters as the active life and the contemplative life.

notes: περισπάω (Luke 10:40, imperfect περιεσπᾶτο): 'to be pulled/drawn about, distracted' per standard lexicons. Confirm form and pronunciation.
Active and contemplative lives: the reading goes back to early writers (often traced to Origen and Augustine, later Gregory the Great). Stated generally as 'some early writers'. Confirm.
Index hook says 'one thing is needed'; the carry uses the KJV 'one thing is needful', as the index does.
Reviewer: changed 'in a room full of men' (not in the text) to 'one many readers think was usually kept for men'. How unusual a woman disciple at a teacher's feet was is debated; confirm framing.
The Martha of John 11 is assumed to be the same Martha; most readers take them as the same family. Confirm framing.
